explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. Paul says to keep away from any brother who "leads an undisciplined life that is not in keeping with the tradition you received from us" (2 Thessalonians 3:6). He gives the command in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, so it carries weight. It's like a recipe card handed down to you, and tossing it out halfway through the batch isn't creative, it's a mess.

Good news for the curious, friend: asking questions isn't what verse 6 is about. The command is about a brother who "leads an undisciplined life that is not in keeping with the tradition you received from us" (2 Thessalonians 3:6). The problem named there is how he lives, not how many questions he asks. I ask questions all day in my bakery, so I'm glad that's not on the list.

Verse 6 doesn't say a word about travel, friend. It says to keep away from a brother who "leads an undisciplined life that is not in keeping with the tradition you received from us" (2 Thessalonians 3:6). Nobody's getting a lecture over a solo road trip in this verse. The command is about how a brother lives.

Paul says the opposite, friend. His team did not "eat anyone’s food without paying for it" (2 Thessalonians 3:8). In the verse before, he says, "we were not undisciplined among you" (2 Thessalonians 3:7). Picture the guest who turns up the minute the cookies leave the oven and never brings a thing. Paul's team was not that guest.

You got it, baker. Paul says his team did not "eat anyone’s food without paying for it" (2 Thessalonians 3:8). They paid their way while they were with the church. In verse 7 he adds, "we were not undisciplined among you." No freeloading on that team.

Burden is the word, friend. Paul says they worked "so that we would not be a burden to any of you" (2 Thessalonians 3:8). Think of a full tray of cookies that somebody else has to haul across the bakery. Paul's team didn't want to be that tray.

Stranger is a fair guess, friend, but the word in verse 8 is "burden." Paul says they worked "so that we would not be a burden to any of you" (2 Thessalonians 3:8). Nothing in that verse mentions strangers. The team just didn't want to weigh anybody down.

Rival sounds like a bake-off, friend, but verse 8 has no competition in it. Paul says they worked "so that we would not be a burden to any of you" (2 Thessalonians 3:8). A burden is a heavy load somebody else has to carry. That's the weight they didn't want to put on anyone.

explanations.answer: To be an example to imitate
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Paul says, "Not that we lack this right, but we wanted to offer ourselves as an example for you to imitate" (2 Thessalonians 3:9). They had the right to be supported and worked anyway. It reminds me of showing a new cutter how to press clean and lift straight. Telling is nice, but doing it where they can see sticks better.

explanations.answer: To prove they were the strongest
explanations.explanation: Nobody's flexing in these verses, friend. The reason Paul gives is that "we wanted to offer ourselves as an example for you to imitate" (2 Thessalonians 3:9). Proving strength never comes up. The example is the whole reason he states.

explanations.answer: To save up for the next trip
explanations.explanation: Verse 9 has no travel fund in it, friend. Paul gives the reason himself: "we wanted to offer ourselves as an example for you to imitate" (2 Thessalonians 3:9). He says they had the right to be supported and worked anyway. Saving for a next trip isn't mentioned there.

explanations.answer: Anyone unwilling to work shall not eat
explanations.explanation: That's the command, friend. Paul says they gave it even while they were with the church: "If anyone is unwilling to work, he shall not eat" (2 Thessalonians 3:10). Short, punchy and no way to misread it. I wish all my recipes were that clear.

explanations.answer: Anyone who works shall rest each week
explanations.explanation: A weekly rest sounds lovely, friend, and I'd sign up, but that's not what verse 10 says. The command is "If anyone is unwilling to work, he shall not eat" (2 Thessalonians 3:10). Paul is talking about work and eating there. There's no day off in this one.

explanations.answer: Anyone who eats shall share with others
explanations.explanation: Sharing is a beautiful thing, friend, but it isn't in verse 10. Paul's command is "If anyone is unwilling to work, he shall not eat" (2 Thessalonians 3:10). It ties working and eating together. The sharing answer sounds good, it just isn't what he said there.

That's right, friend. Paul writes, "we hear that some of you are leading undisciplined lives, accomplishing nothing, but being busybodies" (2 Thessalonians 3:11). Word had reached him, and he says it plainly. Busy, but not getting anything done. That's a full calendar and an empty cookie tray.

Paul says it right there in verse 11: "we hear that some of you are leading undisciplined lives, accomplishing nothing, but being busybodies" (2 Thessalonians 3:11). So "accomplishing nothing" is exactly what he says about them. The news had reached him, and he puts it plainly. I'd frost a cookie, but he doesn't frost this news.

Quietly is the word, friend. Paul commands and urges them by our Lord Jesus Christ "to begin working quietly to earn their own living" (2 Thessalonians 3:12). No announcements, no big update to the group chat, just roll up the sleeves and start. I think that lands extra after the word "busybodies" in verse 11.

Harder sounds like a gym poster, friend, but the word in verse 12 is "quietly." Paul urges them "to begin working quietly to earn their own living" (2 Thessalonians 3:12). The text doesn't ask for more effort. It's about how they work.

Together is a sweet idea, friend, but verse 12 says "quietly." Paul urges them "to begin working quietly to earn their own living" (2 Thessalonians 3:12). The text says nothing about doing it as a group. The point is earning their own living.

explanations.answer: Don't get tired of doing good
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Paul writes, "But as for you, brothers, do not grow weary in well-doing" (2 Thessalonians 3:13). Doing good can be a long batch, and hour six is where the feet start to ache. Paul says keep going.

Rushing isn't in verse 13, friend. Paul says, "do not grow weary in well-doing" (2 Thessalonians 3:13). That's about not wearing out while doing good. A rushed cookie is a sad cookie, but that one's my rule, not Paul's.
There's no bragging in verse 13, friend. Paul says, "do not grow weary in well-doing" (2 Thessalonians 3:13). I once bragged about a batch before it left the oven. The oven had notes.

That's it, friend. Paul says, "do not regard him as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother" (2 Thessalonians 3:15). To admonish is to warn, like a friend tapping you on the shoulder. The church keeps its distance, yet he's still a brother. I think that leaves the door open.

Paul says the opposite, friend. Verse 15 reads, "do not regard him as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother" (2 Thessalonians 3:15). Even with the distance in verse 14, he's still a brother. No opposing needed.

Following him isn't the idea, friend. Verse 14 describes someone who does not obey the instructions in the letter, and verse 15 says to "admonish him as a brother" (2 Thessalonians 3:14-15). He's a brother to admonish, not a leader to follow. Tough to follow someone you're busy admonishing.

Not quite, friend. Paul writes that the Lord of peace may give them peace "at all times and in every way" (2 Thessalonians 3:16). All times covers the easy days too, not only the hard ones. Sunny days, stormy days, burnt-batch days. He covers the whole calendar.

You got it, baker. Paul writes that the Lord of peace may give them peace "at all times and in every way" (2 Thessalonians 3:16). There's no limit to hard times in that sentence. Every hour on the clock counts, even the mornings when the oven won't light. Then he adds, "The Lord be with all of you."

Right on, friend. Paul says, "This is my mark in every letter; it is the way I write" (2 Thessalonians 3:17). He handles the greeting in his own hand. A stamper knows about marks. I press my mark into every cookie so you know who made it.

Paul says it plainly, friend. The greeting is in his own hand, and he says, "This is my mark in every letter; it is the way I write" (2 Thessalonians 3:17). So it's his mark in every letter, not a one-time thing. Think of a signature cookie that you can spot across the room.
